turns.name: W2-dyn
turns.question: You said the app saves the intent with a client transfer ID before it sends anything — what exactly gets written to Room at that moment, and how does the result screen use it while the request is still in flight?

card.problem: Design a mobile wallet: core mobile experience, the system behind it, and how it handles failures; start by clarifying requirements and defining the MVP user path
card.constraints: ["MVP is sending money to a contact (person-to-person), not paying a business", "The server ledger is the single source of truth; the app only shows confirmed entries", "Signed-in users, centralized balance accounts, single currency USD, internal peer-to-peer transfers, zero fees", "Balance, transfer, history and details are in scope; cached reads work offline, submitting money needs the network", "Top-up, withdrawal and multi-currency are out of scope", "A has 100 dollars and B has zero"]
card.heard: what gets written to Room, and how the result screen uses it in flight
card.say: At that moment I write one row: the client transfer ID, the payer and payee, the amount as 8000 cents, and the status "pending". I write it before the request goes out, so a crash can't lose it. The result screen reads that row from Room and shows "processing" while the request is in flight. It only changes to success when the server's transfer record comes back.
card.then: Next: what the server does when the same client ID arrives twice.

more: The row also has a created time and a "last checked" time. The result screen collects that row from Room, so it shows "processing" straight away, even after a restart. When the server's record comes back, I update the same row to success or failure. The screen never reads the status from anywhere else.

turns.question: Separate scenario. A still has 100 dollars. On two phones A approves two independent 80 dollar transfers to B at almost the same time. What happens to each one and what do the phones show?

card.say: These are two separate intents, so each phone makes its own client transfer ID. The server handles them one at a time, because both need the same row for A's balance. It locks that row, or does a conditional update that only takes 8000 cents if the balance is still enough. The first one commits, so A goes from 100 dollars to 20 dollars and B goes from 0 to 80 dollars. The second one finds only 20 dollars left, so it fails cleanly and no money moves.

If that second response is lost, the phone shows unknown and keeps the row pending. On retry it resends the same client transfer ID, and the server returns the original failure.

transcript: Interviewer: Hi, I'm the founder of ActAI. We're building an agent-first mobile communication app, focused on how people talk, coordinate and work together every day. Today we'll start with a project you really owned, then design a fictional mobile wallet together. I'll add a few new conditions along the way, and leave time for your questions at the end.
Interviewer: Pick the one project that best shows your mobile skills. Who used it, what problem did it solve, and where did your responsibility start and end?
Candidate: The project I owned most was the AI trip planner at KKday.
Candidate: I was the technical lead for a five-person team.
Candidate: Travelers typed a destination, a budget and a number of days, and the AI built a trip they could book.
Candidate: I designed the agent, connected it to our product and order data, and wrote the core backend.
Candidate: We streamed the plan day by day, so users saw day one first.
Interviewer: On the AI trip planner at KKday, you said you designed the agent and wrote the core backend — of that, what did you personally build versus what did the five-person team own?
Candidate: Personally, I designed the agent and wrote the core backend.
Candidate: I also wrote the Android code that reads the streamed plan.
Candidate: The other four people owned the app screens, the product rules and the testing.
Candidate: So my responsibility ended where their screens and product decisions began.
Interviewer: Pick a change you personally made. Walk me from one user action through the UI, data or network path. Which logic did you actually change?
Candidate: The change I made myself was the Android side of the streamed plan.
Candidate: When the user sends the request, the app opens the SSE connection and reads the events as they arrive.
Candidate: Each event is one day card or one product card, and I parse it and update the screen through StateFlow.
Candidate: So day one shows up while the rest is still being made.
Candidate: Parsing runs on Dispatchers.IO, and the parsed result is pushed into a StateFlow that the screen collects, so the UI thread never blocks while the next event is still arriving.
Interviewer: What was the hardest bug to reproduce there? What did you suspect first, and which log, experiment or repro proved you wrong?
Candidate: The hardest one was a duplicate day card.
Candidate: Sometimes the same day showed twice, but only on slow networks.
Candidate: I first suspected the backend was sending the event twice.
Candidate: Then I logged every event id and the arrival time on the client.
Candidate: The log showed one event, but my parser ran twice when the connection reconnected.
Candidate: So the bug was mine, not the backend's.
Candidate: The log showed one event from the server, but my parser ran twice when the connection reconnected.
Candidate: So the bug was mine, not the backend's.
Candidate: I fixed it by ignoring an event id I had already handled, and I kept the last id so a reconnect could resume from there.

Interviewer: You said the log showed one event but your parser ran twice on reconnect — how did you confirm the duplicate came from the reconnect path and not, say, a second collector or a re-emitted StateFlow value?
Candidate: I checked it in three steps.
Candidate: First, I logged the collector count, and it stayed at one.
Candidate: Second, I logged every StateFlow emission, and each value came once.
Candidate: Third, I forced a reconnect by cutting the network, and the duplicate appeared right after it.
Candidate: So the extra parse came from the reconnect path, not from a second collector or a re-emitted value.
Candidate: The server would need to keep the events for a short time, so a resume can replay them.
Interviewer: What other options did you have, why didn't you pick them, and after release how did you know the change worked?
Candidate: I had two other options.
Candidate: One was to let the backend send the whole plan at once, and the other was to deduplicate on the server only.
Candidate: I didn't pick the whole plan because users would wait for everything before seeing anything.
Candidate: I didn't pick server-only deduplication because the client still reconnects on its own, so the app has to be safe by itself.
Candidate: After release, I checked the crash-free rate and the ANR rate, and I watched for duplicate day cards in the logs.
Candidate: I also went through the flow myself on a slow network and forced a reconnect.
Candidate: I also checked the duplicate rate in the logs after release, and it stayed at zero.
Candidate: One more thing I'd add now: if the app is killed mid-stream, the last id should survive process death.
Candidate: I'd save it in Room, and the server would replay from there.

Interviewer: Tell me about a time you saw a delivery risk or a likely delay and the team disagreed. When did you tell whom, how many options did you give, who decided, and what did you finish yourself?
Candidate: At KKday, the risk was the release date of the trip planner.
Candidate: The app team was waiting on the backend format, and we were close to the date.
Candidate: I told my team lead and the product manager the same day I saw it.
Candidate: I said the format wasn't agreed yet, so the app couldn't start.
Candidate: I gave two options.
Candidate: One was to fix the card format first and start the app a few days later.
Candidate: The other was to ship with a simpler card and add the rest after.
Candidate: My team lead and the product manager decided.
Candidate: The second option was to ship a simpler card first and add the rest after.
Candidate: My team lead and the product manager chose that one, so the app could start on time.
Candidate: I finished the Android stream reader and the day card myself, so day one could show while the rest was still coming.
Interviewer: You chose to ship the simpler card first — what risk were you knowingly accepting there, who watched the data after release, and what signal would have made you pause or roll back?
Candidate: The risk was that users saw a plan with fewer details, and some product cards came later.
Candidate: I accepted that, because a plan they could start reading was better than a blank screen.
Candidate: After release, I watched the duplicate rate in the logs, plus the crash-free rate and the ANR rate.
Candidate: I'd pause or roll back if duplicates came back, or if the crash-free rate dropped.
Candidate: A clear rise in users editing or re-requesting the same day would also make me stop and look.
Candidate: I'd pause the rollout if the duplicate rate went above zero again, or if the crash-free rate dropped or the ANR rate went up.
Candidate: One more signal: if many users edited the same day again and again, that would tell me the simpler card wasn't enough.

Interviewer: Let's switch to the design exercise. Design a mobile wallet from scratch: the core mobile experience, the system behind it, and how it handles failures. Start by clarifying the requirements. Which user path would you define as the MVP?

Candidate: Thanks, that's clear.
